As the horizon extends, the increasing point estimates imply that the fundamental drivers of growth or appreciation are expected to exert a more significant influence over longer periods, leading to a higher predicted value, albeit at a relatively modest pace.

The widening of the 90% confidence intervals is a direct reflection of the increasing uncertainty inherent in forecasting further into the future. The broader range encompasses a wider array of plausible outcomes as the future becomes less predictable.

While these intervals capture the most likely range of outcomes under normal circumstances, certain specific risks or events could push the actual results outside these predicted bounds. These typically involve high-impact, low-probability occurrences that are difficult to model within standard probabilistic frameworks. Examples include sudden and severe economic downturns or booms, unexpected regulatory changes, significant geopolitical crises, major technological disruptions that rapidly alter market dynamics, or widespread natural disasters. Any event that fundamentally shifts the underlying assumptions driving the forecast—such as a global recession or a completely unanticipated innovation—could lead to outcomes significantly lower or higher than even the widest part of the one-month forecast interval.
